headings.title: Introduction to Health History in Haematological Nursing
headings.content: Taking a comprehensive health history is a fundamental cornerstone of haematological nursing. The blood and lymphatic systems are intricately connected to every organ in the human body, meaning that blood disorders often present with vague, multisystemic symptoms rather than localized complaints. For nursing students in Nigeria, mastering the health history interview allows for early identification of life-threatening conditions such as severe anaemia, bleeding disorders, and malignancies like leukaemia or lymphomas. A thorough health history provides a chronological narrative of the client's health status, contextualizing physical assessment findings and guiding targeted laboratory investigations. It involves establishing therapeutic communication, demonstrating cultural sensitivity, and recognizing that haematological conditions carry significant social and psychological burdens within the West African context. Furthermore, a systematic approach ensures that critical clues regarding genetic predispositions, nutritional deficiencies, and environmental or occupational toxins are not overlooked. By understanding the foundational principles of haematological history taking, student nurses develop clinical reasoning skills that directly impact patient outcomes, reduce complications, and support comprehensive care planning tailored to the individual needs of patients presenting with blood dyscrasias.

headings.title: Biographical Data and Demographic Factors
headings.content: Biographical data and demographic factors serve as essential baseline elements in the haematological health history. Age, gender, ethnicity, occupation, and geographical residence often provide vital diagnostic clues. For instance, in Nigeria and across Sub-Saharan Africa, genetic blood disorders such as sickle cell disease (SCD) and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency have high regional prevalence and distinct ethnic distributions, making demographic inquiry indispensable. Age is another critical variable; certain leukaemias and myelodysplastic syndromes predominantly affect older adults, whereas acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and congenital coagulopathies are more commonly diagnosed in childhood and adolescence. Gender plays a role in X-linked recessive disorders like haemophilia A and B, which primarily manifest in males, while females may be carriers or experience heavy menstrual bleeding leading to iron-deficiency anaemia. Occupational and residential histories must also be evaluated within demographics; exposure to agricultural chemicals, industrial solvents, or living in malaria-endemic zones can heavily influence haematological parameters such as red and white blood cell counts. By carefully evaluating biographical data, nurses can tailor their clinical suspicion, anticipate specific diagnostic differentials, and provide culturally and demographically competent care to their patients.

headings.title: Chief Complaint and History of Present Illness
headings.content: The chief complaint (CC) and history of present illness (HPI) form the core narrative of the patient's current haematological distress. Patients with blood disorders frequently present with complaints related to tissue hypoxia, bleeding tendencies, or immune suppression. Common chief complaints include chronic fatigue, generalized weakness, shortness of breath on exertion, dizziness, easy bruising, recurrent infections, bone pain, or unexplained fevers. When exploring the history of present illness, the nurse must use systematic questioning—such as the PQRST or OLDCARTS mnemonics—to elicit precise details about the onset, location, duration, characteristics, aggravating and relieving factors, and associated symptoms. For instance, if a patient reports fatigue, the nurse must determine when it started, how severely it interferes with daily activities, and whether it is accompanied by pallor or jaundice. For bleeding complaints, details regarding the frequency of epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, or petechiae are essential. Understanding the timeline helps differentiate acute crises, such as a painful vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease, from chronic insidious declines in haemoglobin levels. Documenting the HPI accurately assists the multidisciplinary healthcare team in formulating a precise diagnostic and therapeutic plan.

headings.title: Systemic Review of Symptoms in Blood Disorders
headings.content: A systematic review of systems (ROS) in haematological nursing enables the clinician to uncover subtle manifestations of blood disorders across every bodily system. Because haematological components circulate throughout the entire body, abnormalities can affect the integumentary, neurological, cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and immune systems. In the integumentary system, nurses should inquire about pallor, jaundice, petechiae, purpura, and pruritus. Neurological reviews may reveal headaches, tinnitus, vertigo, peripheral neuropathies (as seen in vitamin B12 deficiency), or confusion resulting from severe anaemia or hyperviscosity. Cardiovascular and respiratory systems must be assessed for palpitations, tachycardia, orthopnoea, and dyspnoea, which indicate the heart's compensatory mechanisms against reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. Gastrointestinal inquiries should focus on glossitis, angular cheilitis, dysphagia (Plummer-Vinson syndrome), abdominal fullness from splenomegaly, or occult blood loss via melena. Musculoskeletal assessments target bone pain, which is characteristic of multiple myeloma or bone marrow packing in leukaemias. Finally, evaluating the immune system involves asking about the frequency, severity, and duration of recurrent infections, poor wound healing, and persistent lymphadenopathy. Conducting a thorough ROS ensures that no systemic clue is missed during the nursing assessment.

headings.title: Past Medical and Surgical History
headings.content: Past medical and surgical history provides essential context for interpreting current haematological findings. The nurse must inquire about previous diagnoses of anaemia, bleeding disorders, malignancies, autoimmune diseases, or chronic kidney disease, as erythropoietin deficiency in renal failure frequently leads to secondary anaemia. A history of blood transfusions should be documented meticulously, noting any previous transfusion reactions, the frequency of past transfusions, and any resulting alloimmunization, which is particularly critical for patients with sickle cell disease who require frequent blood products. Surgical history is equally important; previous splenectomy dramatically alters immune function and increases susceptibility to encapsulated bacterial infections, requiring specific vaccination histories. Furthermore, a history of gastrointestinal surgeries, such as gastric bypass or bowel resection, can impair the absorption of vital haematopoietic nutrients like vitamin B12 and iron, predisposing the patient to megaloblastic or iron-deficiency anaemias. Chronic infections, such as HIV, malaria, or hepatitis, must also be noted because they can suppress bone marrow function or cause secondary hypersplenism and haemolysis. Documenting these past medical and surgical milestones helps nurses connect historical health events to present haematological disruptions.

headings.title: Family and Genetic History
headings.content: Family and genetic history is a pillar of haematological nursing assessment because many blood disorders are inherited through Mendelian or complex genetic patterns. The nurse must construct a detailed multigenerational pedigree or family tree, inquiring about ancestral origin, consanguinity (which is culturally relevant in certain populations), and specific haematological conditions among blood relatives. Key hereditary conditions to screen for include sickle cell anaemia (HbSS, HbSC), thalassaemias, haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, and hereditary spherocytosis. Additionally, a family history of malignancies, such as leukaemias, lymphomas, or multiple myeloma, should be carefully documented, as genetic predispositions and familial cancer syndromes can elevate an individual's risk. Understanding the inheritance pattern—such as autosomal recessive transmission in sickle cell disease or X-linked transmission in haemophilia—enables nurses to provide appropriate genetic counseling referrals, educate family members regarding carrier testing, and anticipate potential clinical complications in offspring or siblings. By exploring the family health background, the nurse bridges individual patient care with broader genetic health education and preventive nursing strategies.

headings.title: Medication History and Toxic Exposures
headings.content: Medication history and toxic exposures provide vital clues regarding drug-induced haematological toxicities and secondary blood dyscrasias. The nurse must conduct a comprehensive reconciliation of all prescribed medications, over-the-counter drugs, herbal preparations, and traditional remedies used by the patient. In Nigeria and many parts of West Africa, the concurrent use of herbal concoctions and traditional remedies alongside conventional drugs is widespread and must be assessed non-judgmental. Certain medications and substances are notorious for causing drug-induced bone marrow suppression, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, or haemolysis. For example, individuals with G6PD deficiency can experience acute haemolytic anaemia when exposed to specific drugs such as antimalarials (e.g., primaquine) or sulfonamides. Anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents (like aspirin and clopidogrel), and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) directly impact coagulation and can precipitate severe bleeding episodes. Furthermore, a thorough occupational and environmental exposure history must investigate contact with known bone marrow toxins, such as benzene, radiation, lead, and agricultural pesticides, which are strongly linked to the development of aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, and acute leukaemias. Documenting these exposures allows nurses to identify reversible causes of haematological abnormalities and educate clients on safe pharmacological practices.

headings.title: Psychosocial, Nutritional, and Lifestyle History
headings.content: Psychosocial, nutritional, and lifestyle history rounds out the holistic health assessment in haematological nursing. Blood disorders—especially chronic conditions like sickle cell disease, haemophilia, and blood cancers—impose immense psychological stress, financial strain, and social stigmatization on patients and their families. The nurse should evaluate coping mechanisms, support systems, mental health status (screening for anxiety and depression), and the impact of the illness on the patient's education, employment, and quality of life. Nutritional history is equally critical because deficiencies in iron, vitamin B12, folate, and protein directly impair erythropoiesis and cause nutritional anaemias. The nurse should explore dietary patterns, including adherence to vegetarian or restricted diets, food security, and cultural dietary practices. Finally, lifestyle factors such as alcohol consumption, cigarette smoking, and recreational drug use must be assessed. Smoking can cause polycythaemia secondary to chronic carbon monoxide exposure or worsen vascular complications in sickle cell disease, while excessive alcohol intake can suppress bone marrow function and contribute to nutritional deficiencies. Incorporating psychosocial and lifestyle dimensions ensures that the nursing care plan addresses the whole person rather than just laboratory values.
